sections.heading: Effective context is a fraction of nominal

slides.title: Long context is not *memory*
slides.text: The window limits what can be sent, not what will be found.

narration: A model's context window is how much it can read at once.
Most leading models now read a million tokens in a single call.
That is between five and seven hundred thousand words.
It invites a simple idea: skip the memory and give the model everything.
This page shows why that does not work for enterprise data.
The window is a limit on what can be sent.
It is not a promise about what will be found.

slides.caption: Most leading models read a million tokens in one call. That invites skipping the memory. Models get worse at finding things long before the window is full.

slides.title: What we will *cover*

narration: First, how standard the one-million-token window has become.
Then the two ways vendors price it.
Then the evidence that effective context is a small fraction of the nominal window.
Then what the studies of long context against retrieval found.
Last, what one ten-million-token prompt costs at list price.

slides.caption: The one-million-token window is standard. Two pricing regimes. Effective context is a fraction of nominal. Long context against retrieval. What ten million tokens costs.

slides.title: The window is *standard*
slides.unit: model families offer a million tokens or more; one claims ten million

narration: As of 13 September 2026, nine model families offer a context window of a million tokens or more.
The list includes every large model vendor, several open-weight families, and two Chinese providers.
One open-weight model claims ten million tokens.
Its claim and its useful length turn out to be very different numbers.
We come to that in a moment.

slides.caption: As of September 2026, nine model families offer a million tokens or more. One claims ten million. The claim and the useful length are different numbers.

slides.title: Two pricing *regimes*

narration: Pricing has split into two regimes.
Some vendors bill flat across the whole window.
A nine hundred thousand token request costs the same per token as a nine thousand token one.
Others bill the whole request at a higher rate once it passes a threshold.
One doubles the input rate past 272 thousand tokens.
Another doubles past 200 thousand.
A third triples past 256 thousand.
The regime matters more than the headline rate for a memory workload.
A memory workload is, by definition, on the wrong side of the threshold.

slides.caption: Some vendors bill flat across the window. Others bill the whole request at double once it passes a threshold. Memory workloads sit on the wrong side of the threshold.

slides.title: Effective context is a *fraction*
head: Model
Claimed
Effective
At 32K
slides.text: Effective means keeping 85 percent of the short-context score. ICML 2025.

narration: One benchmark hides a needle whose words do not match the question.
The model must reason rather than match.
Effective length is the longest context at which a model keeps 85 percent of its short-context accuracy.
A model that claims one million tokens keeps that accuracy to 16 thousand.
One that claims 128 thousand keeps it to 8 thousand.
A model that claims 200 thousand keeps it to 4 thousand.
A model that claims two million keeps it to 2 thousand.
And the model that claims ten million keeps it to 1 thousand.
At 32 thousand tokens it scores 21.6 out of 100.
Eleven of the thirteen models tested fell below half their short-context accuracy by 32 thousand tokens.
No later independent test has contradicted the pattern.

slides.caption: One test removes word overlap between question and evidence. On it, effective context is 1K to 16K for models that claim 1M to 10M.

slides.title: Four more lines of *evidence*
items: Sharp drops past the needle test

narration: Four other lines of evidence say the same thing at different lengths.
A 2024 suite of thirteen tasks found almost every model near perfect on the plain needle test.
Then almost all dropped sharply with length.
Only about half were satisfactory at 32 thousand tokens.
A 2025 suite of 59 models found that no synthetic test predicts real downstream tasks.
Open-weight models collapsed on citation tasks at 128 thousand tokens.
A vector database vendor tested eighteen models in July 2025.
Every one degraded with input length.
A focused prompt of 300 tokens beat the full 113 thousand token history on every model.
And one model vendor's own engineering guidance from September 2025 says it plainly.
As the tokens in the context window increase, the model's ability to recall from it decreases.

slides.caption: Almost all models drop sharply past the plain needle test. Synthetic tests do not predict real tasks. Every model degrades with length. The vendors say so themselves.

slides.title: The 2026 follow-ups reach a *million*
slides.text: The leader at 128K is not the leader at 1M.

narration: The 2026 follow-ups extend this to the million-token range.
A May 2026 study tested 26 models.
The leader at 128 thousand tokens was not the leader at one million.
Seven models moved two or more ranks between the two lengths.
A second May 2026 study watched frontier models miss dangerous actions.
After 800 thousand tokens of ordinary activity, they missed them two to thirty times more often.
A June 2026 study of long searches found models giving up well before the window was full.
The rate rose with length.

slides.caption: The leader at 128 thousand tokens is not the leader at one million. Frontier models miss dangerous actions far more often after 800 thousand tokens.
slides.picture: A podium where the tallest runner at the short race stands lower at the long race.

slides.title: Long context against *retrieval*

narration: What about the studies that compare long context with retrieval directly?
Within the window, long context wins on accuracy.
A 2024 comparison found it ahead by 7.6 points with one frontier model and 13.1 with another.
It loses on cost.
A June 2026 study measured 73.1 percent correct for long context against 65.4 for retrieval.
At twenty-six times the per-question token cost.
The 2024 study proposed routing between the two.
That cut cost by 39 to 65 percent.
Both results hold only for corpora that fit the window.

slides.caption: Within the window, long context wins on accuracy by 7 to 13 points. It loses on cost by ten to twenty-six times. Past the window, plain retrieval collapses too.

slides.title: Past the window, *both* collapse

narration: The picture changes past the window.
A January 2026 benchmark tests question answering over four sizes of corpus.
At 128 thousand tokens the best models score above 80.
At one million, the best scores 50.7.
At four million tokens, plain retrieval scores 2.4.
A memory agent that plans and searches scores 22.1.
At ten million, retrieval scores 1.2 and the memory agent 11.1.
Nothing is good at ten million.
But the shape is clear.
Whatever works there is not one call over the corpus, and not one retrieval either.

slides.caption: A 2026 benchmark tests question answering over 128 thousand to ten million tokens. At four million, plain retrieval scores 2.4 and a memory agent 22.1. At ten million, 1.2 and 11.1.

slides.title: What ten million tokens *costs*
slides.unit: US dollars per ten million input tokens, list price, September 2026
slides.text: Model names, thresholds and cache rates are on the sources page.

narration: What does one ten-million-token prompt cost at list price?
The table is arithmetic on published prices, at the rate above each threshold.
The cheapest one-million-token model charges ten cents per million.
Ten million tokens cost one dollar.
A second budget model costs a dollar and a half.
A mid-tier frontier model at two dollars per million costs twenty dollars.
A preview model that doubles past 200 thousand costs forty.
The largest models cost one hundred, two hundred and six hundred dollars for the same prompt.
The spread is six hundred to one.
And no one-million-token model accepts ten million tokens in one call.
The prompt would have to be split.
These are token-volume costs, not a single request.

slides.caption: At list price, one ten-million-token prompt costs between one dollar and six hundred dollars. No one-million-token model accepts it in a single call.

slides.title: Caching helps a *static* corpus
slides.text: Three cents to twenty dollars, if the same tokens come back.

narration: Most vendors sell a cached read at a fraction of the input price.
A cached read of ten million tokens costs between three cents and twenty dollars.
One pro tier gives no cache discount at all.
Caching helps only when the same tokens are asked again within the cache lifetime.
That is true for a static corpus.
It is not true for a memory that grows every day.
A memory workload serves a team many times a day.
And prices change quarterly.
The sources page records the access date and what to re-check.

slides.caption: A cached read of ten million tokens costs three cents to twenty dollars. It helps only when the same tokens are asked again within the cache lifetime.

slides.title: What to *remember*
items: Cost tiers start where memory begins
Neither one call nor one retrieval

narration: Here is what to remember.
A context window sets the upper bound on one call.
It is not evidence that the call will find what is in it.
Effective context for evidence that does not share words with the question is measured in thousands of tokens.
Not millions.
Cost scales with tokens sent.
The long-context price tiers are set exactly where memory workloads begin.
The two published results at ten million tokens agree.
Neither one call nor one retrieval works there.
What does is the open question on the next page.

slides.caption: A window bounds one call and proves nothing about what will be found. Effective context is thousands of tokens, not millions. Cost tiers start where memory workloads begin.
